OVERVIEW (1 paragraph to write)
─────────────────────────────────
Problem framing: CNS gene therapy has been bottlenecked by (a) the
absence of human substrates for pre-clinical delivery screening and
(b) the gap between model systems (iPSC, mouse, NHP) and the human
cortex that drugs ultimately target. Our ex vivo human brain slice
culture platform addresses this gap directly by using surgically
resected tissue to screen AAV capsid and enhancer libraries at the
cellular resolution of the human brain. <PRELIM: 2-3 sentences on
our preliminary dataset — number of specimens, viability window,
library size screened, headline hits.>

AIM 1 — Platform / infrastructure
─────────────────────────────────
Rationale: AAV capsid and enhancer engineering as a reproducible substrate for library
screening requires characterizing fidelity, viability, and
inter-specimen variance.

1a. Benchmark slice viability and transcriptional fidelity across
    <SAMPLE: n specimens from m anatomical regions> at D0, D7, D14
    using snRNA-seq + snATAC-seq, with comparison to matched acute
    dissociations.
1b. Define the operational window — which cell types remain
    transcriptionally stable, which drift — and lock the SOP for
    downstream library screens.
1c. Deliverable: a public resource (data + SOPs) that other labs
    can adopt.

AIM 2 — Discovery
─────────────────
Rationale: CNS gene delivery benefits directly from screening in
the real target substrate.

2a. Apply our barcoded AAV capsid library (n = <PRELIM: library
    size>) to slices from <SAMPLE> and recover
    capsid-by-cell-type tropism matrices via scRNA-seq.
2b. Apply the enhancer library in parallel and identify
    cell-type-restricted drivers for <TARGET CELL TYPES — e.g.,
    L5 ET neurons, inhibitory PV interneurons, microglia>.
2c. Validate the top <N> hits with single-vector in situ
    experiments.

AIM 3 — Translational handoff
──────────────────────────────
Rationale: a platform earns its keep by producing substrates for
others. This aim turns Aim 2's hits into a shareable toolkit.

3a. Package the top capsid × enhancer combinations as a public AAV
    catalog with vector maps, titers, and expression data.
3b. Pilot one combination in a disease-relevant assay — <CHOICE:
    human AVM tissue, epileptic cortex, GBM resection margin> —
    to show line-of-sight to clinical relevance.
3c. Deliverable: shared vectors + data at <REPOSITORY> within year
    <N> of the award.

INVESTIGATOR / ENVIRONMENT
──────────────────────────
JP McGinnis, MD PhD, is uniquely positioned at the intersection of
operative neurosurgery and vector biology: direct, same-day access
to human CNS tissue; established computational pipeline (published
atlas, snATAC harmonization preprint); existing collaborations with
[Allen Institute, Deliverome/Radial, Parallel Squared]; independent
faculty appointment at BCM July 2027.

title: Eligibility
purpose:
Can I contact BWF to determine my eligibility?
Applicants are required to complete a pre-application eligibility check within ProposalCentral. Only upon completion and confirmed eligibility can the full application be accessed. Please see the “Application Instructions and Submission Guidelines” section of the RFP for more information on how to complete. BWF recommends completing the eligibility check by September 15, 3:00pm EDT. Beyond this date, BWF will not be responding to eligibility inquiries.

Do I need to be nominated by my institution to apply?
No, you do not need to be nominated; however, you must obtain approval from your institution. As of August 2015, eligible candidates may self-nominate by submitting a full proposal by the deadline. All applications must be approved by an official at the institution responsible for sponsored programs (typically from the Grants and Contracts office, the Office of Research, or the Sponsored Programs Office).

I hold a Ph.D. degree only. Am I eligible to apply to the CAMS program? No. If your background is in the physical/mathematical/computational sciences or engineering and your work addresses biological questions, you may want to consider applying to BWF’s Career Awards at the Scientific Interface .

I hold a Pharm.D. or Pharm.D, Ph.D. degree. Am I eligible to apply to the CAMS program? No.

Is 75 percent of the time devoted to researching a firm policy? Yes. Programs and department chairs must provide adequate protection for the candidate to conduct research.

As a surgeon scientist can I be considered with less than 75% research effort? No, currently for the CAMS award the 75% effort is the expectation regardless of specialty. However, if you do not currently have 75% protected time towards research, but it can be negotiated if CAMS were awarded, you may proceed with your application. Please ensure a letter of support or offer letter can demonstrate this in writing before proceeding.

title: Proposal
purpose:
Do I need to create an NIH-style biosketch in SciENcv?
No.  We ask that you submit an NIH-style biosketch, but we do not require that it is made and certified in SciENcv.  You have flexibility to craft an NIH-style biosketch in a manner that is most convenient to you, utilizing past NIH templates or the template in ProposalCentral for your submission if you prefer.

Can I have a co-investigator on this proposal? No. The CAMS grant program does not allow co-investigators.

I have two postdoctoral mentors. Can I submit two mentor recommendation letters? Only one mentor letter of recommendation may be submitted with your proposal application. This letter should be from the person designated as your primary postdoctoral mentor or faculty sponsor in the application.
If you have a co-mentor/secondary mentor, and if both your primary and secondary mentor wish to co-write and sign one mentor letter, that is also acceptable.
Alternatively, if you have a co-mentor/secondary mentor and they would like to write one of your three additional recommendation letters, that is also acceptable.

Can support letters be sent separately outside the grant application? No. All support letters must be uploaded and attached to your application and submitted electronically by the application deadline. Emailed, mailed, or faxed letters will not be accepted.

To whom should my letters of recommendation be addressed? Letters of recommendation should be addressed to the CAMS Advisory Committee and must be uploaded and attached to your application and submitted electronically by the application deadline. Emailed, mailed, or faxed letters will not be accepted.

If I attach a bibliography to my research plan, does it count toward the six-page maximum? No. Also, glossaries of technical abbreviations and terms are acceptable and encouraged if they clarify the proposal to the general reader and do not count toward the page limit.

title: Application
purpose:
Is the BWF application deadline firm? Yes.
Applications will not be accepted after 3:00 pm EDT on September 30, 2026. At the precise deadline, the online application system will gray out the SUBMIT button preventing submission and will NOT be reactivated.

Can I submit a paper application? No. BWF requires that all applications for this program be submitted electronically by the application deadline. Paper applications will not be accepted.

Can I submit more than one application? No.

Can I change my application once it is submitted? No. Once your application is submitted, it cannot be changed.

What is a “signature block”? A signature block is found at the end of a letter and includes the letter writer’s name, title(s), department(s), and institution. It is usually found just after the closing of the letter (e.g., just after the word ‘Sincerely,’ or ‘Yours truly,’) and just under the letter writer’s signature. Here is an example of a signature block:
Jane Smith, M.D., Ph.D. Chair and Professor, Department of Medicine ABC University

Do I need to complete an application in one session? No, you can start an application and return later to complete it. When beginning a new application, you are required to log in with an existing or established proposal central log-in and password. You can save, exit the application, and return later at any time during the application process.

I forgot my user ID and/or password. What should I do? If you have forgotten your password or user ID, visit the BWF grant application system and click the forgotten password link.

title: Award Logistics
purpose:
Can I change institutions during the award? The award is portable.  Most awardees will change institutions to begin a faculty appointment. However, transferring your award is not guaranteed. The institution that you wish to transfer to must demonstrate a commitment to you by offering you a tenure track or equivalent faculty appointment and significant start-up money. In addition, BWF must approve the transfer of funds. Transfers during the faculty portion of the award are discouraged.

Can I interrupt the award because of family commitments? Yes.  Awardees may receive annual no-cost extensions; requests explaining why an extension is needed must be submitted in writing at least four months before the end date of the award.

Are awardees permitted to receive other simultaneous funding, such as from the National Institutes of Health or another foundation? Award recipients may obtain funds from other sources for research in the same or similar areas as that conducted under these grants, so long as there is no conflict with meeting the terms of BWF’s award. Award recipients may not hold concurrent BWF awards or NIH K99/R00, NIH DP5, or similar Early Independence awards.

What are my chances of receiving a Career Award for Medical Scientists? There is no way to know definitively how many proposals we will receive each application cycle and, therefore, what the success rate will be. Based on the number of eligible applicants in the 2025-2026 cycle (156) and awards given (12), the funding rate was 7.7 percent.

underlying spatial and temporal regulation of NaV1.8 channels are technologically innovative. UbiquiNaV will

title: [Funded ref] Neural Mechanisms of Interocular Suppression in Marmoset Visual Cortex
purpose:
PROJECT SUMMARY The ability to perceive a coherent and unified visual scene requires the brain to
integrate inputs from the two eyes. However, the retinal images from each eye often differ due to perspective,
occlusion, or lack of overlap in the periphery. Under such conditions, rather than fusing these incompatible
inputs, the brain suppresses one eye’s contribution—a phenomenon known as interocular suppression. Binocular
rivalry (BR), where incongruent images presented to each eye produce alternating percepts, provides a
compelling behavioral demonstration of this suppression. Primary visual cortex (V1) is thought to play a key role
in interocular suppression. Current models posit that mutual inhibition between eye-specific neuronal
populations in V1, mediated by local inhibitory interneurons, underlies the suppression of one eye’s input.
However, accumulating evidence suggests that top-down feedback (FB) from higher visual areas also contributes
to this process, modulating V1 activity to bias perceptual outcomes. The relative contribution of these two
mechanisms—local inhibition versus top-down modulation—remains poorly understood. This proposal aims to
elucidate the circuit-level mechanisms that mediate interocular suppression in V1 by developing a novel
marmoset monkey model. The marmoset shares key features with the human visual system—including a foveal

purpose:
Abstract
 Juvenile Open-Angle Glaucoma (JOAG) is a rare condition characterized by severely elevated intraocular
pressure (IOP), progressive visual field loss, and a high risk of blindness. Current treatment options, such as
daily eye drops and invasive surgeries, fail to address the underlying pathology of trabecular meshwork (TM)
dysfunction. Especially in younger children, medication adherence remains a critical issue. Even for adult open
angle glaucoma patients, daily eye drop administration is often a struggle. To address this critical unmet need,
Diorasis Therapeutics (DTx) proposes a first-in-class, disease-modifying gene therapy that targets TM
dysfunction to normalize aqueous humor outflow and reduce IOP. Unlike gene-specific approaches, this therapy
utilizes adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors to deliver an enzymatically inactive variant of tissue plasminogen
activator, a key regulator of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling
in the TM. This approach targets the site of pathology but only reduces IOP when elevated, avoiding any potential
for hypotony.

complementary AAV2-PLATvector (which encodes a tPA variant), achieving IOP normalization in >90% of treated

all ALS patients regardless of genetic etiology and initial muscular onset. Remarkably, extraocular eye muscles

been studied from the neuronal or muscular perspective, but glial contribution remains largely understudied. An

title: [Funded ref] Development of a PET Imaging Platform to De-Risk AAV Gene Therapy Clinical Trials
sponsor: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
purpose:
Abstract
Genetic diseases affect 1% of live births. Although each individual disorder is rare, collectively they affect millions
of Americans. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapies treat genetic disorders by hijacking a virus’
machinery to deliver a therapeutic transgene to patients. The transgene expresses an essential protein that may
be missing or defective in patients inflicted by 1 of the 6,000 known genetic disorders. Despite this exciting
breakthrough, limited knowledge of AAV pharmacokinetics leads to a critical barrier—high clinical development
risk, hindering the development of new therapies.
We propose to monitor AAV gene therapy pharmacokinetics using a common imaging modality called positron
emission tomography (PET) to provide early signs of success/failure in large animal models and early clinical
trials, thereby mitigating risks of resource-intensive late-stage clinical trials. To achieve this, a novel PET reporter
gene will be developed and co-delivered with the therapeutic transgene by AAVs, enabling non-invasive
transgene biodistribution and persistence tracking over time.
Specific aims include: 1) PET reporter optimization and 2) PET reporter evaluation in vivo. Successful completion
will pave the way for the development of a clinical platform that improves AAV gene therapy clinical trial success
rates.

sponsor: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
purpose:
Abstract
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is the most severe and lethal skeletal muscle disease in the human
population. Although the DMD-causing mutation has been known for 30+ years, there is still no effective cure

Abstract

phenotypes. Sleep behavior is no exception since it is believed that multiple genes contribute to total sleep

identified a gene (CACNA1D) encoding a voltage gated calcium channel. Seven of the 34 families each had one
novel variant co-segregating with the FASP trait in this highly conserved gene. There are 6 such variant alleles

on to perform in vitro experiments showing functional consequences of these variants. We have generated a

title: [Funded ref] Elucidating the Cellular and Molecular Basis of Fibroinflammation
sponsor: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
purpose:
Project Summary
Fibrosing diseases of the skin are highly morbid conditions with a large unmet medical need. These diseases are strongly
associated with tissue inflammation (termed ‘fibroinflammation’). It is thought that both the quality and quantity of these
inflammatory reactions play a major role in dictating whether fibrosis will occur and how severe it will be. The cellular
and molecular pathways that drive fibroinflammation remain to be fully elucidated. We have discovered that CD8+ T cells
play a major role in driving fibroinflammation. In addition, we have identified a novel population of skin fibroblasts that
are highly responsive to inflammatory cytokines and rapidly expand in this context. The central focus of this grant
application is to elucidate the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which CD8+ T cells and the newly discovered Pi16
expressing fibroblasts (PiFs) contribute to fibroinflammation. We hypothesize that when there is a reduction in tissue
immune regulation, CD8+ T cells kill adipocytes, either directly through adipocyte-specific antigen recognition or
indirectly through secretion of cytokines that adipocytes are exquisitely sensitive to. We further hypothesize that in
this setting, both type 1 and type 2 immune responses activate PIFs and drive them towards a pro-inflammatory
and pro-fibrotic state. The combination of adipocyte death and activation of PIFs work in concert to create a unique
microenvironment that facilitates pro-fibrotic inflammation

PROJECT SUMMARY
Tick species such as Ixodes scapularis are major vectors of bacterial pathogens, including Lyme disease and

do not address vector competence, or the ability for ticks to harbor and transmit these pathogens. One major
factor controlling vector competence is the tick immune response to infection, of which mechanistic knowledge
is profoundly lacking. To develop effective, targeted methods to prevent tick-borne disease before patients
become sick, a far greater understanding of tick immune pathways is necessary. We recently discovered that

with multiple signaling networks, including the IMD pathway, which impact vector competence. Preliminary data
indicate that IKKε phosphorylates the IMD pathway core regulator XIAP. In Aim 1, IMD-activating interactions
between IKKε and XIAP will be characterized by performing molecular and biochemical interaction assays and
by applying Cas9-mediated gene editing and targeted mutagenesis techniques.

title: [Funded ref] Project 2: RB as a gatekeeper of lineage plasticity
purpose:
Project Summary/Abstract
 An increasingly recognized mechanism of resistance to targeted therapies for adenocarcinomas is the
emergence of cancer cells with neuroendocrine (NE) features. NE cancer cells are not only resistant to the initial
targeted therapy (e.g., EGFR inhibition for lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), and AR inhibition for prostate
adenocarcinoma (PRAD), but also to many other therapeutic approaches, leading to low overall survival rates.
A common feature in nearly all adenocarcinomas that undergo this transition is loss of the RB tumor suppressor.
Our group recently provided conclusive evidence that RB loss in the initial adenocarcinoma is required for
subsequent NE transition using genetically engineered mouse prostate cancer models. Collectively, the data
support a model whereby RB loss in adenocarcinomas establishes a cell state “poised” for lineage transition, but
the molecular details underlying this new cell state and how RB loss promotes this state are poorly understood.

downstream events are required for transition to a full NE state but these are largely unknown.

title: [Funded ref] Understanding and targeting treatment-associated lineage plasticity in cancer
purpose:
Project Summary/Abstract
Despite tremendous progress in cancer treatment over the past two decades, resistance to therapy remains a
major cause of cancer mortality. The overarching hypothesis of this P01 is that therapy resistance arises
through aberrant re-activation of developmental programs that normally establish and maintain cell identity and
constrain plasticity. Their dysregulation in cancer disrupts cellular identity and promotes lineage plasticity. We
further hypothesize that some of these plasticity mechanisms are shared across cancers and are best elucidated
through comparative analyses. We will focus on two distinct malignancies—lung and prostate cancer—to identify
both common and context-specific mechanisms of plasticity. Notably, although lung and prostate cancers differ
markedly in disease progression and clinical features, therapy resistance in both cancers frequently occurs via
transdifferentiation of adenocarcinoma to neuroendocrine states. Mice are essential for the proposed work as
they allow us (1) to investigate developmental phenotypes that cannot be studied in patients, (2) to probe in vivo
cellular and molecular mechanisms of cell plasticity that also cannot be studied in patients, and (3) to test new
therapeutic strategies in a pre-clinical setting for future clinical translation. Importantly, we complement these
studies in mice with the analysis of patient samples and experiments with human tumor organoids.

title: [Funded ref] Causes and Effects of Somatic Mutation in Parkinson’s disease
purpose:
Project Summary
 This project aims to study somatic mutations in the human brain in Parkinson’s disease (PD), a
common age-associated neurodegenerative disorder in the United States. A major gap in the field of PD
research is the incomplete understanding of the mechanisms of neuron loss in this disease. Somatic mutations
arise in cells of multicellular organisms, either during development or postnatally. DNA repair pathways have
evolved to protect the genome by preventing somatic mutations because virtually all cells rely on an intact
genome. PD displays increased oxidative stress, DNA damage, and neuron cell death, but whether somatic
mutations play a role in PD pathology, the mechanisms that might cause such mutations, and their exact
functional consequences, are unknown.

sponsor: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
purpose:
Project Summary

understood. As OA progresses, synovial fluid pH drops below 6.4, exposing chondrocytes to acidic stress that

chondrocyte during OA-induced acidosis and elucidate the mechanisms underlying its regulation of joint

title: [Funded ref] Analysis of cis-regulation in synthetic and genomic enhancers
sponsor: National Institute of General Medical Sciences
purpose:
PROJECT SUMMARY
A majority of heritable disease-causing variation resides in the non-coding portions of the
genome. The leading hypothesis is that these variants perturb the functions of cis-regulatory
elements, such as enhancers. Our field has made strong progress identifying the DNA-binding
specificities of the transcription factors that comprise enhancers. Based on these specificities, the
field has also made strong progress identifying enhancers in the genome. However, we still lack
robust models that predict the effects of sequence variations on enhancer activities. Our
hypothesis is that this lack of predictive power stems from a lack of understanding of 1) the
cooperative and competitive interactions within enhancers between sites for different transcription
factors, 2) the interactions between enhancers and their chromatin environments, and 3) the
interactions between enhancers and their cell-type specific trans environments. We aim to identify
and quantify these types of interactions with the goal of improving models that predict the effects
of genetic variation on gene expression.

purpose:

title: [Funded ref] X-ray Pulse Programming: Redefining the Temporal Dimension of CT Imaging
sponsor: National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering
purpose:
PROJECT SUMMARY
Computed tomography (CT) is a cornerstone of modern medical imaging, producing high-resolution, three-
dimensional pictures of the body in seconds. In dynamic or perfusion CT—used to visualize blood flow in the
brain, heart, and tumors—dozens of scans are taken over time to track how contrast dye moves through
tissues. Although these time-series images are highly redundant, with most anatomy remaining unchanged
between frames, current scanners treat each scan independently and use a fixed pattern of X-ray pulses that
ignores this built-in overlap. As a result, the scanner wastes radiation measuring the same structures
repeatedly, while still missing rapid changes during critical phases of contrast enhancement.
This project introduces X-ray pulse programming, a new framework that uses programmable control of every
X-ray pulse in time, angle, and intensity. By coordinating pulse timing with the patient's physiology, the scanner
can allocate more sampling during fast contrast changes and less during steady periods, while also using prior
knowledge from earlier scans to reconstruct the next image more efficiently. The same total dose can therefore
yield higher temporal resolution and cleaner images, or the dose can be reduced substantially without loss of
diagnostic accuracy.

title: [Funded ref] Myeloid lineage commitment during stress hematopoiesis
sponsor: National Heart Lung and Blood Institute
purpose:
ABSTRACT
Hematopoiesis starts with pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), which gradually restrict their lineage
potential through multipotent progenitor cells (MPP), producing hematopoietic lineages and, eventually, mature
blood cells. Increased demand for a specific cell population, e.g. neutrophilic granulocytes and monocytes during
bacterial infection, is met by a partially understood response program (referred to as stress or emergency
hematopoiesis) that increases cell generation and release of required cell types, typically at the expense of less
needed blood lineages. This bias is usually short-lived and compensated upon cessation of the demand;
however, in chronic situations, such dysregulation may lead to non-physiological sequelae. In fact, as emerging
over the last few years, it appears that such mechanisms are at play in a growing number of chronic, etiologically
diverse diseases, such as periodontitis, stroke, polytrauma and aging-associated inflammation (inflammaging).
Common denominators of these examples are the critical roles of IL-1 and monocytes, as determined by detailed
animal models, suggesting that various peripheral insults converge on the activation of IL-1, which in turn drives
neutrophils/ monocyte-production and pathology. While the role of IL-1 in stress hematopoiesis is thus well
established, the molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways that IL-1 uses to control a balanced cell output
during stress hematopoiesis are less well understood.

title: [Funded ref] Mapping Feedforward and Feedback Signaling in Human Speech
sponsor: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders
purpose:
PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
Speech production relies on the brain’s ability to predict and monitor self-generated sounds, ensuring accurate
vocalization and real-time error correction. A key neural mechanism supporting this process is the corollary
discharge, a feedforward predictive signal thought to originate in the speech motor cortex and influence auditory
perception. One well-documented consequence of this mechanism is speech-induced auditory suppression,
where auditory cortex activity is reduced during speaking compared to hearing. Disruptions in the corollary
discharge circuit have been implicated in stuttering, where leading theories propose that instability or inaccuracy
in this signal disrupts the smooth execution of speech. Importantly, when auditory feedback is altered, the brain
generates an error signal to adjust speech output. However, the neural dynamics of this process are not well
understood. Impaired integration of error signals with sensorimotor outputs is also thought to underlie speech
dysfluencies in conditions such as stuttering. This project aims to (1) identify the cortical source of corollary
discharge communication and its role in auditory suppression and (2) determine how auditory error signals
propagate to the speech motor system to drive compensatory adjustments.

circuits are uniquely specialized in the primate inferior temporal cortex to carry out object identification.

title: [Funded ref] Immune reprogramming with bioengineered scaffolds for the treatment of biofilm infection
sponsor: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
purpose:
A craniotomy is a common neurosurgery where a portion of the skull is removed (bone flap) to access the brain
for procedures that include tumor resection, resection of epileptogenic foci, and aneurysm clipping, where the
bone flap is replaced intraoperatively. Nearly 1 million craniotomies are performed in the US annually, which
increases to ~14 million worldwide. Despite prophylaxis, infectious complications after craniotomy average from
1-3%, with upwards of 15% depending on the institution. Over 75% of infections are due to gram-positive
Staphylococci, with approximately 50% attributed to Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), which forms a biofilm
on the bone flap. Therefore, considering the volume of craniotomy procedures, the incidence of craniotomy
infection is significant. Currently, there are no existing methods to treat craniotomy infections without surgical
interventions because the biofilm elicits aberrant immune responses. Systemic antibiotics require weeks to
months for therapeutic levels to accumulate in the brain, which is inefficient and may promote antibiotic
resistance, microbiome dysbiosis, and other adverse side effects. Therefore, there is a critical need to develop

dehydrogenase wild-type (IDHwt) GBM remains resistant to current treatment modalities, with median survival

regions compared to conventional imaging modalities. This technique has enabled characterization of differential
expression patterns of key pH regulatory mechanisms, including monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1/4),

sponsor: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
purpose:
PROJECT SUMMARY
 Chronic pain is a major healthcare problem, affecting 20% of the population and costing society
approximately $600 billion dollars per year. Intracranial neuromodulation therapies such as deep brain
stimulation have great therapeutic potential, but their development is hindered by a poor understanding of
brain circuits underlying pain. Identifying pain-specific brain circuits is challenging because of the confound
of salience. Salient stimuli, such as a surprising loud sound, are defined as those that are highly distinct
from the environment. They typically evoke several reflexive processes including increased attention,
preparatory motor activity, and sympathetic arousal, such as pupil dilation. Painful stimuli are generally
highly salient and evoke widespread activation in neural circuits that process salient stimuli (including non-
painful stimuli, e.g., a surprising, loud sound). Thus, there is a need to identify neural circuits that are specific
for pain, as distinguished from neural circuits for salience, to inform future targeted brain stimulation
protocols for the treatment of chronic pain. Our central hypothesis is that nociceptive stimuli evoke pain-
